extracted.intended_audience: students and competitors in mathematical olympiads / contest problem solvers (advanced high-school and undergraduate level)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and methods for proving inequalities: a catalog of standard techniques (AM-GM, Cauchy–Schwarz, rearrangement, convexity, normalization, trigonometric substitution, etc.) together with illustrative examples and contest problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform expressions to positive pi (e.g., xi^2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to transform the inequality into the form pi, pi > 0, e.g., pi = xi^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make substitutions that render terms manifestly nonnegative (squares, positive parameters) to enable application of standard inequalities or comparison arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize AM/GM/HM/QM patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the expression remind you of the AM, GM, HM, or QM?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search for direct applications of elementary mean inequalities; sometimes rewriting or grouping terms reveals a mean relation that yields the desired bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Cauchy–Schwarz frequently
rubrics_metrics.description: Can you apply the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality? This is especially tricky. You can apply this inequality far more often than you think.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for scalar-product or sum-of-squares structures; consider introducing auxiliary sequences to apply CS, square and sum relations, or use CS variants (Titu's lemma, rearranged CS).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the Rearrangement inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: Can you apply the Rearrangement inequality? Again, this theorem is much underused. You can apply it in most unexpected circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When variables are similarly or oppositely sorted, arrange sequences to maximize/minimize scalar products; consider symmetric sums and ordering assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit symmetry by ordering variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the inequality symmetric in its variables a, b, c, ...? In that case, assume a ≤ b ≤ c ≤ .... Sometimes one can assume that a is the maximal or minimal element. It may be advantageous to express the inequality by elementary symmetric functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fix an order to reduce cases, use extremal element arguments, or express in symmetric polynomials to simplify. This often reduces dimensionality of search for equality cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalize homogeneous inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: An inequality homogeneous in its variables can be normalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scaling freedom (e.g., set sum = 1, product = 1, or max = 1) to reduce parameters and simplify the inequality; normalization can make use of classical inequalities easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangle-side substitution for triangle inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are dealing with an inequality for the sides a, b, c of a triangle, think of the triangle inequality in its many forms. Especially, think of setting a = x + y, b = y + z and c = z + x with x, y, z > 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the standard parameterization a = x+y etc. to turn triangle constraints into positivity constraints and exploit symmetry; also use sine/cosine/area relations when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce to f(variables) ≥ 0 and examine quadratics/discriminants
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring the inequality into the form f(a, b, c, ...) ≥ 0. Is f quadratic in one of its variables? Can you find its discriminant?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat f as a univariate quadratic in one variable (with other variables fixed), ensure discriminant ≤ 0 or show coefficient/sign structure that guarantees nonnegativity; this often converts inequality to checking a discriminant condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use induction for integer-indexed statements
rubrics_metrics.description: If the inequality is to be proved for all positive integers n ≥ n0, then use induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up a base case and show how assuming the inequality for n yields it for n+1, possibly by algebraic manipulation or bounding techniques; sometimes proving a stronger statement helps the inductive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate by telescoping series or products
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to make estimates by telescoping series or products: (a2 − a1) + (a3 − a2) + · · · + (an − an−1) = an − a1, and likewise for product telescoping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-express sums/products as telescoping to obtain tight bounds; split complicated expressions into differences or ratios that collapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use product/sum extremal principles (AM-GM style)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a1 x1 + · · · + an xn = c, then x1·...·xn is maximal for a1x1 = ... = anxn. If x1·...·xn = c, then a1x1 + · · · + anxn is minimal for a1x1 = ... = anxn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use equality conditions of AM-GM or Lagrange multipliers intuition: balance weighted terms to maximize/minimize products or sums under linear constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean/Extremal argument: if mean > d then max > d
rubrics_metrics.description: Max xi > d if the mean of the xi is > d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple average-based reasoning can show existence of large/small elements; use contrapositive arguments on bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positivity by sum/mean arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: One of several numbers is positive if their sum or mean is positive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use global sums/means to deduce sign existence for individual terms; useful in combinatorial or sign-based inequality problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use convexity/concavity
rubrics_metrics.description: A powerful idea for proving inequalities is convexity or concavity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove convexity/concavity of a function in relevant variables and apply Jensen's inequality, midpoint/vertex arguments, or reduce to checking extrema at boundary points; convexity also justifies replacing variables by averages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solve as an optimization problem (minimize/maximize T)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove an inequality T(a, b, c, ...) ≥ 0 or ≤ 0 one often solves an optimization problem: find the values a, b, c, ... such that T is a minimum or maximum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reinterpret inequality as an extremal problem; use calculus, Lagrange multipliers, convexity, or combinatorial extremal methods to find minima/maxima and verify inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigonometric substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Does trigonometric substitution simplify the inequality?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use substitutions such as xi/(xi+yi) = sin^2 θ etc., or represent ratios by trig functions to exploit identities and bounds like cos ≤ 1, cos(a−b) ≤ 1; particularly useful for rational expressions and triangle problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: If standard methods fail, transform until one applies
rubrics_metrics.description: If none of these methods is immediately applicable then transform the inequality into a simpler form with some aims in view until a standard method is applicable. If you have no success, continue transforming and try to interpret the intermediate results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iteratively manipulate the expression, try substitutions, homogenization, bounding, or consider related inequalities; persistence and reinterpretation often reveal a path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use convexity plus compactness to reduce extrema to vertices
rubrics_metrics.description: When a function is (strictly) convex on a closed bounded convex domain, its maximum/minimum is assumed at the extremal points (vertices) of the domain (Weierstrass theorem cited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this to problems where variables lie in a cube or polytope (e.g., 0 ≤ ai ≤ 1): a convex objective attains extrema at vertices, reducing continuous problem to a finite combinatorial check. Examples: US Olympiad 1980 problem and the tetrahedron edge-sum problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check equality cases explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: In many proofs the authors determine when equality holds, often phrased 'We have equality iff ...' (e.g., equality for the equilateral triangle when a = b = c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and verify the necessary and sufficient conditions for equality—this helps validate sharpness of constants and guides substitution choices that attain bounds.
